newsitem.title: USA: US bean, corn acres seen higher than budget number.
newsitem.headline: US bean, corn acres seen higher than budget number.

text.p: U.S. soybean and corn acreage and production in 1997 will likely be higher than the numbers included in the administration's proposed budget, Agriculture Department analysts said Thursday.
And 1997 wheat plantings will probably be lower than the figures used in the budget, they said.

"The market shouldn't react too much to the budget assumption," said an analyst who did not want to be identified. He and other analysts noted that these numbers were based on November conditions, and that more information has been learned since then.

The fiscal 1998 budget proposed by the White House Thursday included four-month-old assumptions for U.S. crops. Based on November 1996 conditions, the projections assumed plantings of 64 million acres of soybeans, 81.5 million acres of corn and 72 million acres of wheat.

Analysts stressed that January's historically low winter wheat acreage estimate of 48.2 million acres was not taken into account in the budget, and that these low planting intentions will impact all major crop acreage.
"It would be consistent to expect higher soybean and corn numbers," said one analyst.

Industry expectations for 1997 plantings have been as high as 65.2 million acres for soybeans and 81.3 million acres for corn. Analysts said those numbers are based on more current information than the budget and "are probably more likely."
Wheat acreage will likely be lower than 72 million acres, analysts said.

Experts said with the projected low winter wheat acreage of 48.2 million acres, a spring wheat acreage equal to last year would be necessary to hit 72 million acres of all wheat, and they said that "may be hard to match."

"Obviously we're thinking a little tighter than that (72 million acres) now, based on wheat seedings that came out in January. Winter wheat acreage of 48.2 million acres would not be consistant with the 72 million acre number."
The Agriculture Department will release its first projections of 1997 acreage and production later this month at the department's annual outlook conference.
